segments.he: רבינו ז"ל אמר שאם היו"כ אינו כראוי (היינו שלא יכול להתפלל ביו"כ כראוי) אז השם ה' יהי' כראוי "אז דער יו"כ איז ניט גווען ווייא עס בדארץ ציא זיין זאל חאטשי דער גאסט נאבין זיין וויא עס בדארץ ציא זיין" (היינו מחרת יו"כ שנקרא בפי העולם שם ה' כידוע): היינו שיהי' התחזקות אפי' ביו"כ שאז הזמן מוכשר מאד לתשובה ולא עבר כראוי יחזק א"ע ומתי שיעשה טוב הוא טוב וכן אומרים אנ"ש (בשם מהרנ"ת) אפי' כשכל השמ"ע לא התפלל כראוי עכ"פ יתפלל אלקי נצור כראוי וכו':
segments.en: Concerning Reb Moshe Klain — one of our fellowship born in Eretz Yisroel who drew close to Rabbainu through disciples of Moharan'as: Reb Meir of Teplik and Reb Nachman of Avrohovsky, whose father lived in their neighborhood. His mother was pregnant with him and gave birth — and they thought he was a stillborn and suffered greatly and did not want to make the circumcision. But the disciples of Moharan'as took the child into their home, performed the circumcision, and promised that he would live a good life. And when the boy grew up he drew close to them and became their disciple. But his father — incited by the opponents — began to persecute him intensely, even to actual physical danger, and sat shiva over him, G-d preserve us, and expelled him from being a son. [They said to him about this: "Because of this I will not sit shiva over any more of my children" — and so it was, that over all his other children who died in his lifetime he sat shiva, but over him he had an unusually long life. And in his old age he was with him in honor and studied Rabbainu's book — and later regretted his opposition, saying he had not known the holiness of Rabbainu and his books.] This Reb Moshe traveled to Uman for Rosh HaShanah. When he was traveling back, it was Purim on the ship. He had a Megillah and they read it — and a Greek gentile passed by and spat on the Megillah. Reb Moshe raised his hand and gave him several proper slaps. The Greek went and complained to the captain — and the captain came with his officers and arrested Reb Moshe. They wanted to punish him and asked him truthfully: "Did you hit this Greek?" He answered yes. They asked why he hit him. He answered: "Because he disgraced and spat on the Ten Commandments." He then opened the Megillah to the passage of the Ten Sons of Haman, where the names are written in large letters, and showed them. He told them these were the Ten Commandments — and they counted the lines and said: "Yes, yes, you spoke truth — these are the Ten Commandments." And they thanked him for the slap and they themselves beat the Greek. [In truth: if he had shown them the Ten Commandments in the Torah scroll they would not have been as obvious, since the large letters in the Ten Sons of Haman are much more visible — and they believed him. And indeed it is written in the holy books that the Ten Sons of Haman correspond to the Ten Commandments.] Reb Moshe ultimately lived in Haifa, engaged in commerce, became wealthy, was generous and charitable — there is much to tell of his charity. And his name became renowned for praise throughout Haifa. And he brought close there a precious soul like himself — Reb Yehudah Rosenthal — whose righteousness, holiness, uprightness, and wholeness became renowned throughout Haifa. There is much to say about these two souls. And Reb Moshe ultimately lost his wealth through a wicked second wife, a relative of his, who robbed all his assets — and he also became indebted. And he wrote to me [asking that a disciple of Reb Yisroel of Kardan go to Reb Yisroel's grave in Tiberias to tell him of his troubles]. And this woman also suffered greatly — she contracted cancer and died from it. And the end was that Reb Moshe fell from his wealth entirely through her, and the house and property were taken for her debts. Out of mercy they rented him a small dark dwelling in a gentile's courtyard — with only one bed that he slept on, full of dirt and insects. And he became ill and weak throughout his body, his eyes dimmed from seeing, and all his limbs ceased to function. He had to go every day to the hospitality house to eat a piece of bread with a little tea — that was his sustenance. And so it was for some time. When we heard of this, trembling seized us and I could not believe it — and I traveled with the arousal of our fellowship and came to his dwelling. I literally could not understand how he could live there even one week, much less so many months. And I did not know him at all. I brought him to Jerusalem among our fellowship, and he was with us from the twenty-fifth of Elul until the twelfth of Nisan, when he passed away. Throughout all that time he never complained or said a word against Hashem — on the contrary, he always justified the Divine decree. When he was in Jerusalem he would tell me all the above and tell me he had been a disciple of Reb Nachman of Avrohovsky and served him — and that the primary arousal for his drawing close came through the letters of Reb Leibele Rubens, which were given to him to copy — and through this he was aroused and drew close to Rabbainu. And he told me he had heard from Reb Nachman that Rabbainu said: "I want to remain among you" — as cited in Chayay Moharan — there is in this an allusion that they should name their children Nachman: "Let each one have a Nachman in his house." "Yeder zol hobn a Nachmele." And he also told me that once Reb Nachman called him to him and said: "I have a request of you — promise me you will fulfill it." He promised. He said: "My request is that immediately after my passing, take the note that I am giving you now — on which I wrote 'bring him to Reb Nachman of Breslov' — and place it in his hand when you bury him, so that he will be buried with the note." And he said he was doing this so that if they ask where to bring him, he would show the note. And he fulfilled as he was commanded. And Reb Moshe had great vitality being among our fellowship, and had lodging near one of our fellowship who watched over him with food. And in the month of Nisan I traveled to Tzfas — and came back on the thirteenth of Nisan to Jerusalem. They told me of his passing — that they had found him in the morning, lying with his hands outstretched upward. And they accorded him the last honors and our fellowship even prayed in his room. And I was distressed that had I been present at his passing I would have done the note for him as he had done for his teacher. And one of our fellowship who had been watching over him with food told me that he had done this on his own initiative — even though he had not heard the story from him and knew nothing of it at all.
